FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions:
WHAT IS THIS DOCUMENT?
This is your Final Explanation guide. By the end of this unit, you should be able to write a complete, evidence-based answer to the driving question using everything you have learned across all 8 lessons. Read this document carefully before you begin writing your response.

YOUR DRIVING QUESTION:
"Why do the aluminium sufuria, the graphite pencil and the table salt on our kitchen table look similar as solids but behave so differently — and what is happening between the atoms inside each one that controls every property we can measure?"

HOW TO USE THIS DOCUMENT:
• Read each section prompt carefully before you write.
• Use the exemplar paragraphs as a model — notice how they link particle-level evidence to observable properties.
• Do NOT copy the exemplars. Use them to guide the structure and depth of your own answer.
• Connect every claim you make back to the anchoring phenomenon (the three items on the demonstration desk).
• Use scientific vocabulary accurately: bond type, lattice, delocalised electrons, electrostatic attraction, layers, ions, melting point, conductivity, malleability.
• Aim for a complete response that addresses all five sections.

sections.title: Section 1 — Identify the Bond Type in Each Substance
sections.prompt: For each of the three kitchen substances — table salt (NaCl), aluminium (Al), and graphite (C) — identify the type of chemical bonding present. Explain what particles are involved in each bond and how the bond forms. Why is it important to identify the bond type before explaining any physical property?
sections.exemplar: The three substances on the demonstration desk look similar as solids, but they are held together by completely different types of chemical bonds — and that difference is the key to everything else we observe. Table salt (NaCl), harvested from the Kenyan coast, contains an ionic bond. This forms when sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, producing a positive Na⁺ ion and a negative Cl⁻ ion. These oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly through electrostatic forces. Aluminium metal contains a metallic bond: the aluminium atoms release their outer electrons into a shared 'sea' of delocalised electrons that flows freely between the positive Al³⁺ ions. Graphite is a form of carbon held together by covalent bonds. Each carbon atom forms three strong covalent bonds with its neighbours in a flat, hexagonal layer. The fourth outer electron from each carbon atom is delocalised across the entire layer. Identifying the bond type matters because the type and strength of the bond directly controls every measurable property — melting point, conductivity, and mechanical behaviour — as we will see in the sections below.

sections.title: Section 2 — Structure at the Particle Level
sections.prompt: Describe the three-dimensional arrangement of particles (the structure) inside each substance. How does this internal structure differ between table salt, aluminium, and graphite? Use the terms 'lattice', 'layers', and 'sea of electrons' where appropriate, and connect each structure back to what you could see or do to the sample on the demonstration desk.
sections.exemplar: The internal structure of each substance explains the shapes and textures we observed on the demonstration desk. Table salt forms a giant ionic lattice: millions of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are arranged in an alternating, three-dimensional grid, held in fixed positions by strong electrostatic attractions in all directions. This is why the salt crystal is rigid and cannot be bent — the ions are locked in place. Aluminium also forms a giant metallic lattice: rows of Al³⁺ ions are packed closely together and surrounded by the free-moving sea of delocalised electrons. Because the electron sea holds the ions together without locking them into one fixed arrangement, the layers of ions can slide over each other when force is applied — which is why the sufuria wire bent without snapping. Graphite has a layered covalent structure: flat sheets of carbon atoms, each bonded in a hexagonal network, are stacked on top of each other. The bonds within each layer are strong, but the forces between the layers are very weak, allowing layers to slide over one another easily. This is exactly why the graphite rod left a grey mark on the paper — thin layers flaked off and stayed behind.

sections.title: Section 3 — Explaining Conductivity (The Circuit Experiment)
sections.prompt: When the teacher connected each substance to a simple circuit with a bulb, the results were surprising. Explain, using particle-level reasoning, why aluminium conducts electricity as a solid, why dry table salt does NOT conduct as a solid but DOES conduct when dissolved in water, and why graphite — a non-metal — also conducts electricity. What does this tell us about what is needed for a substance to conduct electricity?
sections.exemplar: The circuit experiment was the most surprising part of the demonstration, and bond type explains every result perfectly. For a substance to conduct electricity, it must contain charged particles that are free to move and carry charge through the material. Aluminium conducts electricity as a solid because its delocalised electrons are always free to drift through the metallic lattice when a voltage is applied. This is why the bulb lit up immediately when the sufuria wire was placed in the circuit. Dry table salt does NOT conduct electricity because, in the solid ionic lattice, the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are locked in fixed positions by the strong electrostatic forces all around them — they cannot move. However, when salt is dissolved in water, the lattice breaks apart and the ions become free to move through the solution. These mobile ions carry charge and the bulb lights up. This shows that ions can conduct electricity, but only when they are free to move. Graphite conducts electricity even though carbon is a non-metal because each carbon atom contributes one delocalised electron to the layer. These electrons are free to move across the entire sheet of carbon atoms — just like the electrons in a metal. This is why graphite is used as an electrode in batteries and electrolysis cells. The rule we can write is: electrical conductivity requires freely moving charged particles — either delocalised electrons (as in metals and graphite) or free ions (as in ionic solutions).

sections.title: Section 4 — Explaining Melting Point and Mechanical Behaviour
sections.prompt: The teacher showed that table salt melts at above 800 °C, aluminium melts at 660 °C, and graphite layers flake off easily even at room temperature. Also, the aluminium wire bent without breaking, but the graphite rod snapped when force was applied. Use your knowledge of bond type and structure to explain ALL of these observations. What must happen at the particle level for a solid to melt or to be deformed?
sections.exemplar: To melt a solid, you must supply enough energy to overcome the forces holding the particles together. The stronger the forces, the higher the melting point. Table salt has the highest melting point of the three (above 800 °C) because the electrostatic attractions between the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions act in all three directions through the lattice and are extremely strong — a huge amount of thermal energy is needed to pull every ion away from its neighbours. A home jiko burning charcoal in Nairobi cannot produce enough heat to melt salt, which is why it stays solid during cooking. Aluminium melts at a lower temperature (660 °C) because the metallic bonds, though still strong, involve the electrostatic attraction between the electron sea and the Al³⁺ ions in only one type of interaction, and these can be overcome with less energy than the full ionic lattice. For mechanical behaviour, the aluminium wire can bend because the layers of Al³⁺ ions can slide past each other while still being held by the same electron sea — the bond type does not break. This property is called malleability. Table salt, however, will shatter rather than bend: if you push the layers of ions sideways, ions of the same charge are forced next to each other, the repulsion is enormous, and the crystal breaks apart. Graphite flakes easily because the covalent bonds within each carbon layer are very strong, but the forces between the layers are weak. A small force is enough to slide one layer off another — which is why the graphite rod left a mark on paper and why the rod was brittle and snapped when bent.

sections.title: Section 5 — Answering the Driving Question (Your Complete Explanation)
sections.prompt: Now bring everything together. Write a full, connected answer to the driving question. Your answer must: (1) state the three bond types and the three structures; (2) use particle-level reasoning to explain conductivity, melting point, and mechanical behaviour for ALL three substances; (3) explain what was puzzling about the phenomenon at the start and how your understanding of chemical bonding now resolves that puzzle; and (4) state one real-world application or implication of what you have learned — you may use Kenyan examples.
sections.exemplar:
At the start of this unit, we faced a genuine puzzle: three everyday kitchen items — table salt from the Kenyan coast, an aluminium sufuria wire, and a graphite rod from a used battery — all appeared as dull or shiny solids, yet they behaved in completely opposite ways when we tested them for conductivity, melting point, and mechanical strength. The answer to every part of this puzzle lies in the type of chemical bond holding the atoms or ions together, and the three-dimensional structure that bond creates.

Table salt (NaCl) contains an ionic bond: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held in a giant three-dimensional lattice by strong electrostatic attractions in all directions. Because the ions are locked in fixed positions, dry salt cannot conduct electricity. Only when dissolved in water do the ions become free to move and carry charge. The strong, all-directional forces also require over 800 °C to overcome, giving salt its very high melting point, and the rigid lattice makes it hard but brittle.

Aluminium contains a metallic bond: a sea of delocalised electrons surrounds a lattice of Al³⁺ ions. The free electrons allow aluminium to conduct electricity immediately, even as a solid. The metallic bond is strong enough to give aluminium a melting point of 660 °C, but because the electron sea maintains the bond even as ion layers slide past each other, aluminium is malleable — it bends without breaking. This is exactly why aluminium is used to make sufuria handles and cooking pots across Kenya.

Graphite is a covalent structure: each carbon atom forms three strong covalent bonds within a flat hexagonal layer, and one delocalised electron per atom is free to move across the layer. This makes graphite a conductor of electricity — surprising because carbon is a non-metal. Between the layers, the forces are very weak, so layers slide off easily, leaving marks on paper and making graphite useful as the 'lead' in pencils. The layers also make graphite brittle — it snaps rather than bends.

The driving question asked what is happening between the atoms inside each solid that controls every property we can measure. The answer is: bond type determines the arrangement of particles, and the arrangement of particles determines every property. There are no exceptions among the three substances. One important real-world implication is in recycling: aluminium from old sufuria and cooking pots can be melted down and reformed at just 660 °C, making it energy-efficient to recycle in Kenyan industries. Salt, by contrast, would require far more energy to melt, and graphite is used in the electrodes of the very electrolysis cells that are used to purify metals in chemical industries. Understanding chemical bonding is not an abstract exercise — it explains the materials that Kenyans use, recycle, and depend on every day.

rubric.excellent: Correctly identifies ionic bonding in NaCl, metallic bonding in Al, and covalent (+ delocalised electrons) in graphite. Accurately describes the particles involved and how each bond forms, with no errors.
rubric.proficient: Correctly identifies all three bond types and mostly describes the particles involved, with one minor error or omission in the description of bond formation.
rubric.developing: Identifies one or two bond types correctly but confuses the particles involved or omits a key bond type entirely.

rubric.excellent: Accurately describes the giant ionic lattice (NaCl), metallic lattice with electron sea (Al), and layered covalent structure (graphite). Correctly uses 'lattice', 'layers', and 'sea of electrons' and connects each structure directly to observable features of the substances on the demonstration desk.
rubric.proficient: Describes the structure of all three substances with mostly accurate detail. Uses at least two of the required terms correctly and connects at least two structures to the observed phenomenon.
rubric.developing: Describes the structure of only one or two substances, or uses structural terms incorrectly. Makes limited connection to the observed phenomenon.

rubric.excellent: Provides a complete, accurate particle-level explanation for why Al conducts as a solid (free electrons), why dry NaCl does not conduct but conducts in solution (ions locked vs. free), and why graphite conducts (delocalised electrons across layers). Clearly states the general rule about freely moving charged particles.
rubric.proficient: Explains conductivity for all three substances with mostly correct particle-level reasoning. May omit the general rule or provide a partially incomplete explanation for one substance.
rubric.developing: Explains conductivity for only one or two substances, or relies on surface-level observations (e.g., 'it is a metal') without particle-level reasoning.

rubric.criterion: Explaining Melting Point and Mechanical Behaviour
rubric.excellent: Accurately links the high melting point of NaCl to strong all-directional electrostatic forces, Al's lower melting point to the metallic bond, and graphite's flaking to weak interlayer forces. Correctly explains malleability of Al (sliding ion layers in electron sea) and brittleness of NaCl and graphite using particle-level arguments.
rubric.proficient: Correctly explains melting point trends and mechanical behaviour for at least two of the three substances using particle-level reasoning. One explanation may lack full detail.
rubric.developing: Describes the observed behaviours (e.g., 'salt has a high melting point') without connecting them to bond type or particle-level structure, or provides only one correct particle-level explanation.

rubric.excellent: Writes a coherent, complete answer to the driving question that integrates all three bond types, all three structures, and all tested properties. Clearly articulates how chemical bonding resolves the original puzzle. Provides at least one accurate, relevant real-world application using a Kenyan context (e.g., aluminium recycling, graphite electrodes, salt in industry or cooking).
rubric.proficient: Integrates most of the unit's concepts into a connected answer. Addresses the original puzzle and includes a real-world application, though the connection to a Kenyan context may be general or partially developed.
rubric.developing: Provides a partial synthesis that addresses some but not all of the properties or substances. The answer to the driving question is incomplete, and the real-world application is absent or not connected to chemical bonding concepts.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Why do the aluminium sufuria, the graphite pencil and the table salt on our kitchen table look similar as solids but behave so differently — and what is happening between the atoms inside each one that controls every property we can measure?

lessons.title: The Three Kitchen Mysteries: Anchoring the Phenomenon & Eliciting Prior Knowledge
lessons.observed: Students handled and examined three household objects — an aluminium sufuria (or sufuria lid), a graphite pencil, and a pinch of table salt (NaCl) — and recorded observations about their appearance, texture, hardness, and behaviour when tested for electrical conductivity with a simple circuit board. All three appeared as grey/white solids, yet they responded differently: the sufuria conducted electricity readily; the graphite pencil lead conducted weakly; the salt conducted only when dissolved in water. Teachers should note that at this stage students have NOT yet received instruction — the activity is purely phenomenological. Expect surprise and productive confusion, especially about graphite conducting electricity despite being a non-metal.
lessons.learned: Students surfaced and documented prior knowledge and misconceptions about electrical conductivity, melting points, and mechanical properties of common solids. Key baseline ideas that typically emerge include: 'metals conduct, non-metals don't' (a useful but incomplete rule students will refine), 'hard things have high melting points', and 'salt dissolves so it must be soft'. These ideas should be recorded verbatim on the Driving Question Board (DQB) and revisited in every subsequent lesson. Pedagogical note: resist the urge to correct misconceptions now — eliciting them authentically is the lesson's core purpose.
lessons.explained: No formal explanation is constructed in Lesson 1. Instead, the teacher anchors the entire unit by framing the three objects as an unresolved mystery: 'We will spend the next eight lessons building the explanation from the inside out — starting with the atoms themselves.' The teacher introduces the DQB and records the class's best current explanations alongside their questions. Students write an individual 'prediction letter' describing what they think is happening inside each solid; these are sealed and returned in Lesson 8 for self-assessment. Pedagogical note: the prediction letter is a metacognitive anchor — it makes prior knowledge visible and creates a personal stake in the unit's resolution.

lessons.title: Predicting the Invisible: What Are Our Three Kitchen Items Made Of?
lessons.observed: Students retrieved and reviewed the periodic table, focusing on Group 1, Group 6/7, and Group 13 elements relevant to the three kitchen items (Na, Cl, Al, C). Using electron configuration cards (or a projected periodic table), they identified the number of valence electrons for each element and recorded Lewis dot symbols. The teacher used cold-calling (minimum 4 students per question) with 10–15 seconds of wait time before accepting answers, ensuring broad participation. Students then used a structured prediction template to forecast: (a) what type of bonding each substance would exhibit, and (b) which physical properties they would expect as a result.
lessons.learned: Learners activated prior knowledge of valence electrons and electron arrangement from Sub-Strand 2.1. They practised writing structured scientific predictions using the 'I predict… because… and I expect to see evidence of this when…' framework — an NGSS Science and Engineering Practice (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations / Constructing Explanations). Students distinguished between predictions based on reasoning (acceptable) and guesses without justification (not acceptable). Pedagogical note: emphasise that a wrong but well-reasoned prediction is scientifically valuable — this normalises revision of ideas, which is central to the unit.
lessons.explained: Students used their valence electron counts to begin reasoning about WHY atoms might bond: Al has 3 valence electrons it 'wants' to lose; Cl has 7 and 'wants' to gain one; Na has 1 and 'wants' to lose it; C has 4 and could share. Teachers should introduce — but not yet fully explain — the concept of electron transfer vs. electron sharing as two broad bonding strategies. The DQB is updated with new student questions arising from the prediction activity, such as 'If Al gives away electrons, where do they go?' and 'How does carbon hold itself together if it shares equally?' These questions drive Lessons 3–5.

lessons.title: Ionic Bonding: Why Does Table Salt Conduct Only When Dissolved?
lessons.observed: Students carried out a structured conductivity investigation comparing: (a) solid NaCl crystals, (b) NaCl dissolved in water from Lake Turkana (high salinity — a Kenya-relevant context), (c) distilled water, and (d) sugar solution (as a control non-electrolyte). Results were recorded in a class data table on the board. Students also observed (via a projected video or diagram) the cubic crystal lattice structure of NaCl, noting how ions are locked in fixed positions in the solid state but free to move when dissolved. Pedagogical note: the contrast between solid NaCl (no conductivity) and dissolved NaCl (strong conductivity) is the key empirical anchor for the concept of mobile ions.
lessons.learned: Ionic bonds form by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, creating oppositely charged ions (cations and anions) that attract each other electrostatically. The resulting giant ionic lattice has: high melting and boiling points (strong electrostatic forces require large energy input to overcome); brittleness (ion layers shift under stress, bringing like charges together, causing repulsion and cleavage); conductivity only in aqueous solution or molten state (ions must be mobile to carry charge). Students should be able to explain why coastal Kenya communities use sea salt (NaCl) and why it behaves as it does in cooking.
lessons.explained: Students constructed a written explanation for the salt conductivity data using the claim–evidence–reasoning (CER) framework: Claim — NaCl conducts only when dissolved; Evidence — the conductivity data from the investigation; Reasoning — in solid NaCl, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move to carry current, but dissolving in water frees the ions to migrate to electrodes. The teacher should use a physical model (students acting as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, locked arm-in-arm, then 'dissolving' by separating) to make the abstract concrete. Update the DQB: students can now partially answer 'Why does salt dissolve and conduct?' Connect back to the sufuria and pencil — 'Those don't dissolve, so how DO they conduct?'

lessons.title: Valence Electrons, Dot-and-Cross Diagrams, and the Six Bond Types
lessons.observed: Students examined a set of six 'mystery substance' cards (each describing physical properties — melting point, conductivity, solubility, hardness) representing the six bond types: ionic (NaCl), metallic (Al), simple covalent molecular (H₂O), giant covalent/atomic (diamond/graphite), polar covalent (HCl), and non-polar covalent (Cl₂). Working in pairs, students sorted the cards by bond type before receiving any instruction, recording their reasoning. The teacher circulated and used targeted questioning: 'What evidence from the card makes you think that?' and 'Which of the kitchen items behaves most like this mystery substance?' Pedagogical note: the card-sort is a formative assessment tool — collect reasoning notes to identify persistent misconceptions before Lesson 5.
lessons.learned: Students learned the definitions and distinguishing features of all six bond types: ionic (electron transfer, e.g., coastal NaCl from Mombasa salt flats), covalent (electron sharing, subdivided into polar and non-polar), metallic (delocalised electron sea, e.g., the aluminium sufuria), and giant covalent/atomic structures (e.g., graphite and diamond from carbon). The distinction between bond type and structural type was introduced: two substances can share a bond type (e.g., both NaCl and MgO are ionic) but differ in formula and properties. Students practised Lewis dot symbols for Na, Cl, Al, C, H, and O as the foundation for dot-and-cross diagrams in Lesson 6.
lessons.explained: The teacher used a structured comparison table (bond type / what is shared or transferred / example from Kenya context / key property trend) to consolidate the six bond types. Students completed the table collaboratively and then used it to revisit their Lesson 2 predictions, annotating corrections in a different colour pen — a visible record of conceptual change. The DQB is updated: students can now name the bond type for each kitchen item and are ready to ask deeper questions about structure (e.g., 'If Al has a sea of electrons, why doesn't it dissolve like salt?'). Pedagogical note: the structured comparison table doubles as a revision resource for the end-of-unit assessment.

lessons.title: Metallic Bonding and the Aluminium Sufuria: The Electron Sea Model
lessons.observed: Students investigated properties of the aluminium sufuria and a copper wire (both metallic) through a set of physical tests: electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity (warming one end and timing heat travel), malleability (hammering a thin Al foil without shattering), and ductility (stretching a wire). Results were compared against the ionic (NaCl) and covalent (graphite) data gathered in earlier lessons. Students plotted the three substances on a class comparison chart: melting point vs. conductivity. Pedagogical note: the thermal conductivity test connects directly to the everyday experience of burning one's hand on an aluminium sufuria handle — a powerful Kenya kitchen context that makes the phenomenon personally meaningful.
lessons.learned: Metallic bonding involves a lattice of positive metal ions (cations) surrounded by a 'sea' or 'cloud' of delocalised electrons that are free to move throughout the entire structure. This model explains: high electrical conductivity (delocalised electrons move freely under a potential difference); high thermal conductivity (mobile electrons transfer kinetic energy rapidly); malleability and ductility (ion layers slide past each other without breaking bonds, because the electron sea continuously re-bonds them); high melting points (strong electrostatic attraction between cations and the electron sea requires large energy to overcome, though generally lower than giant ionic/covalent structures for lighter metals). Students connect this to why Kenyan jua kali artisans can hammer and shape aluminium sufuria without the metal cracking.
lessons.explained: Students constructed a labelled diagram of the metallic bonding model for aluminium, showing Al³⁺ cations in a regular lattice and the delocalised electron sea. They annotated the diagram to explain each physical property tested. The CER framework was applied: 'Al conducts heat because… the evidence is… the reasoning using the electron sea model is…' The teacher should explicitly address the common misconception that 'metals conduct because they are hard' — hardness and conductivity have different structural explanations. Update DQB: students can now fully explain the sufuria's behaviour. The remaining mystery is graphite — a non-metal that conducts. 'How can carbon form an electron sea without being a metal?'

lessons.title: Seeing the Invisible: Drawing Ionic and Covalent Bonds with Dot-and-Cross Diagrams
lessons.observed: Students practised drawing dot-and-cross diagrams for a progression of molecules and ionic compounds of increasing complexity: H₂ (non-polar covalent), HCl (polar covalent, linking to NaCl comparisons), H₂O (polar covalent, relevant as the solvent in all their conductivity experiments), NaCl (ionic, revisiting Lesson 3 with formal notation), MgO (ionic, used in cooking vessels), and CO₂ (simple covalent, linking to photosynthesis in Sub-Strand 3). Students peer-marked using a provided answer key, identifying the most common error (mixing up dots and crosses from the same atom, or misplacing lone pairs). Pedagogical note: dot-and-cross diagrams are a high-frequency exam skill — budget adequate practice time and use peer-marking to build self-assessment capacity.
lessons.learned: Ionic bonding involves complete electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal, producing oppositely charged ions (e.g., Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in table salt from Kenyan coastal markets). Covalent bonding involves the sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms to achieve full outer shells. Dot-and-cross diagrams represent these electron arrangements: in ionic diagrams, the transferred electron is shown in the new ion's outer shell (using a cross to indicate its origin); in covalent diagrams, shared pairs appear between the two atomic symbols with bonding pairs and lone pairs clearly distinguished. Students can identify bond polarity by comparing electronegativities and can use diagrams to predict the number of bonds an atom will form.
lessons.explained: Students explained how the dot-and-cross diagram for NaCl reveals why the compound is ionic (one atom loses, the other gains — no sharing) while the diagram for H₂O reveals why it is covalent (both atoms share). They connected diagram features to physical properties: ionic compounds have full electron transfer → strong lattice → high melting point; simple covalent molecules have shared pairs but weak intermolecular forces → low melting point (e.g., water melts at 0 °C while NaCl melts at 801 °C). The DQB is updated to note that graphite is covalent but has a very HIGH melting point — prompting the Lesson 7 investigation into giant vs. simple covalent structures.

lessons.title: Bond Types, Structures and Physical Properties: Making Sense of the Data
lessons.observed: Students analysed a compiled class data set (from Lessons 1, 3, 5) alongside a provided reference table of melting points, conductivities, solubilities, and hardness values for: NaCl, Al, graphite, diamond, H₂O, and CO₂. They constructed a scatter plot of melting point vs. bond type and identified the pattern that giant structures (ionic lattice, metallic lattice, giant covalent) cluster at high melting points while simple molecular structures cluster low. Students then examined physical models or 3-D diagrams of graphite's layered hexagonal structure and diamond's tetrahedral network, noting how carbon forms four covalent bonds in diamond but only three in graphite (leaving one delocalised electron per carbon — the key to graphite's conductivity). Pedagogical note: this lesson is the intellectual climax of the unit — allow extended discussion time and resist rushing to closure.
lessons.learned: Each substance has a structural type determined by its bond type: NaCl forms a giant ionic lattice (ions fixed in position → no conductivity in solid state, brittle, high melting point); Al forms a giant metallic lattice (delocalised electrons → high conductivity, malleable, high melting point); graphite forms a giant covalent layered structure (delocalised electrons within layers → conducts, layers slide easily → soft and lubricating, very high melting point); diamond forms a giant covalent network (no delocalised electrons → non-conducting, hardest natural substance, highest melting point). Simple molecular covalent substances (e.g., H₂O, CO₂) have strong covalent bonds within molecules but weak intermolecular forces between molecules → low melting points. The four structural types (giant ionic, metallic, giant covalent, simple molecular) account for virtually all variation in physical properties.
lessons.explained: Students constructed a four-quadrant structural type map, placing each kitchen item and reference substance in the correct quadrant and annotating with the bonding explanation for each property. The map serves as a visual synthesis of Lessons 3–7. The teacher used a Socratic discussion (minimum 6 cold-calls, 15 seconds wait time) to draw out the key generalisation: 'It is not the bond type alone, but the structural arrangement of those bonds across the whole substance, that determines physical properties.' Students annotated their Lesson 2 prediction templates with final corrections, completing the visible record of conceptual change. The DQB is nearly complete — most questions have been answered, setting up the Lesson 8 synthesis.

lessons.title: Final Explanation — Four Structural Types, Jigsaw Presentations and the Complete Story of the Kitchen Items
lessons.observed: Students participated in a Jigsaw activity: expert groups each prepared a 3-minute explanation of one structural type (giant ionic / metallic / giant covalent / simple molecular), then regrouped to teach each other. Each student's jigsaw card included: the structural type, a Kenya-context example, a labelled diagram, and a three-property explanation. Students then retrieved their sealed 'prediction letters' from Lesson 1 and read their original ideas alongside their now-complete understanding. The class conducted a final conductivity and property re-test of all three kitchen items, this time narrating the observations in real time using the bonding vocabulary developed across the unit. Pedagogical note: the prediction letter retrieval is a high-impact metacognitive moment — allow 5 minutes of silent individual reflection before class discussion.
lessons.learned: Across Lessons 2–8, students learned that the differences between the aluminium sufuria, the graphite pencil, and table salt are explained by four giant structural types and their bonding forces. Bond type (ionic, metallic, covalent) determines structural type (giant ionic lattice, metallic lattice, giant covalent network/layers, simple molecular); structural type determines the nature and number of interactions that must be overcome; the energy required to overcome those interactions determines every measurable physical property — melting point, conductivity, solubility, hardness, and malleability. This causal chain (bond type → structure → particle interactions → properties) is the master explanation for the entire unit and the complete answer to the driving question.
lessons.explained: Students wrote individual final explanations answering the driving question in full, using the four-part causal chain as a scaffold: (1) identify the bond type and justify using valence electrons; (2) describe the resulting structural type and draw a labelled diagram; (3) describe the particle-level interactions (electrostatic lattice forces, delocalised electron sea, covalent network/layers, weak intermolecular forces); (4) explain each measured property as a consequence of those interactions. Responses were peer-assessed against a co-constructed success criteria rubric. The teacher closed the unit by returning to the original DQB and ceremonially answering each remaining question, celebrating the class's intellectual journey from kitchen observation to atomic-level explanation. Students updated their Science Notebooks with a final annotated model showing all three kitchen items and their internal bonding structures.
